newsitem.title: USA: House's Archer clashes with Clinton over budget.
newsitem.headline: House's Archer clashes with Clinton over budget.

text.p: The head of the House Ways and Means committee urged President Clinton on Sunday not to play games with statistics that could make a proposed Republican tax bill appear to favour wealthy Americans.
Clinton was scheduled to make remarks on Monday about the budget after the White House said on Friday that both Senate and House bills were unacceptable in their present form.

In a letter, the committee chairman, Republican Representative Bill Archer of Texas, offered to work together with the president on a bipartisan basis but said the White House had wrongly used Treasury Department income data in its calculations of the bill's benefits for middle-class Americans.
"To ensure fairness, I hope you won't rely on any government figures that artificially inflate people's incomes in an effort to make taxpayers appear richer than they really are," Archer said.
The Texas Republican said the White House previously used Treasury Department data that "differs sharply" from economic statistics compiled by other government agencies.
As calculated with congressional data and statistics, the House tax bill would give 71 percent of its tax relief to those who make between $20,000 and $75,000 annually, Archer said.

"I urge you to continue to work with us in the same bipartisan spirit that has brought us this far," Archer said. "It won't be helpful to draw lines in the sand, and I believe all parties should avoid doing so."
The White House and Congress have had a long-running dispute over how to calculate the impact of proposed tax cuts on the middle class and the wealthy.
On Friday the Senate joined the House in approving the biggest tax cut for Americans in 16 years, a five-year net tax cut of about $77 billion in the Senate bill.

Congress passed the tax bills on the heels of spending legislation approved earlier this week. Combined, they would implement a highly touted agreement between congressional leaders and the White House to balance the budget over five years.

White House spokesman Barry Toiv said the administration stood by its use of Treasury Department numbers and argued that congressional Republicans had skewed the benefits of their tax relief toward the wealthy.
"We believe the Treasury numbers are the most accurate," Toiv said.
"Congressional Republicans have underestimated the benefits they provide to the wealthy ... by focusing on the short-term impact instead of the permanent impact of their tax bill," he added.
"In fact, their tax cut is dramatically weighted to benefit the wealthy, and we believe that the bill, not only in the short term but in the longer term, should benefit the middle class," Toiv said.
House and Senate negotiators in coming weeks will seek to work out differences in their tax bills, so they can send a final package to Clinton.
